newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Slow Swiss economy growth seen after 96 drop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Slow Swiss economy growth seen after 96 drop.

text.p: Switzerland's struggling economy shrank in 1996 but may have started reaching bottom in the fourth quarter, officials said on Tuesday.
They forecast that gross domestic product (GDP) could grow by just 0.5 percent this year.

Seasonally adjusted economic output was unchanged in the last three months of 1996, compared with the previous quarter, snapping a string of seven consecutive quarterly drops, the Federal Office for Economic Policy in Berne said.
That followed a revised 0.6 percent fall in the third quarter. It put overall 1996 GDP down a real 0.7 percent compared with 1995, when GDP had edged up by 0.1 percent.

Economists said the economy, which has stagnated since 1990, may be able to show modest growth in 1997 if demand picks up in major European markets and uncertainty about Europe's single currency does not drive the weak Swiss franc sharply higher.
But the upturn seems too weak at this stage to prompt any tightening of Swiss monetary policy soon, they said.
"We expect a rise in 1997 GDP of around 0.5 percent," Hans Sieber, director of the economics office in Berne, told Reuters.
He said fourth-quarter data suggested that the economy was moving through its trough in the winter semester of 1996/97.

"We assume that the second half of 1997 will be better. In particular we expect positive momentum for foreign demand in light of significantly better exchange rates as well as somewhat better economic perspectives in Europe," he said.
This momentum will not be enough, however, to spark a self-sustaining rebound in a domestic economy still undergoing deep structural changes, he added.

"For 1997 we expect only modest overall economic growth, in the first semester continuing stagnation but in the second semester clearly better results. We are emerging from stagnation but one should not be too optimistic," he said.

The official Council for Economic Policy, a government advisory panel, said it was sticking to its forecast from December that GDP would grow 0.5 percent this year, although it now viewed that target as "slightly pessimistic".

It said European Union countries should grow around two percent this year, fuelling demand for Swiss products. The franc, which fell around 12 percent against major currencies in the year to February, is also weaker than expected.
Swiss interest rates remain low as a result of the Swiss National Bank's (SNB) expansive monetary policy, laying the groundwork for recovery, it said.
Alois Bischofberger, chief economist at Credit Suisse Group, said the 0.7 decline in 1996 was exactly in line with the bank's forecast but he detected some surprises in the data.

Investment in corporate equipment was surprisingly strong, growing 8.4 percent year-on-year in 1996, he said, and private consumption was up a relatively robust 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter from the year-earlier period.
"But I see no reason to change our 1997 forecast on the basis of these numbers. We expect a very slight rise in real GDP of 0.3 percent and we are sticking to this prognosis," he said.

The weak franc's impact on foreign demand will probably start showing up in the second half and GDP should continue to grow into 1998, when major export markets like Germany, France and Italy show more dynamic growth, he said.
The latest data is unlikely to provoke any change in the generous monetary policy which the SNB adopted in 1995 and has pressed aggressively since mid-1996, Bischofberger said.
"I would think the SNB can continue its expansive monetary policy in coming months. I would not expect it to become more expansive than it already is," he said.
"Money supply has already grown strongly and even more growth would be undesirable. There is no cause for inflation alarm but you have to keep an eye on imported inflation."

He thought the SNB would only cut its discount rate, now matching a record low 1.0 percent, in the unlikely event that heavy speculation pushed the franc higher and the mark neared the 80 Swiss centime level from current levels around 86.50.

"It seems to me the probability of a discount rate cut is slight. But I would say that we will stay for some time at this low level. I don't think in the next few months we will have a higher discount rate," he said.
